hero.highlight.text: Same cases, same validator, two versions compared case by case.

hero.takeaway.text: Turn the tool tasks of the first three lessons into a fixed case suite and let a program outside the agent judge every case. Run ended, answer correct, evidence sufficient and process violations are recorded separately, and no failed or unassessable case is dropped.

concepts.01-split.description.text: While you change the prompt you rerun the development set; the holdout set is set aside in advance and runs only once a version is chosen.

concepts.02-verifier.description.text: The validator reads only the case spec and this run's trace, never how the agent rates itself. Every criterion that can be written as a program is left to the program.

concepts.03-checks.description.text: Run ended, call comparison, answer correct, evidence sufficient and no process violation each get their own entry; what cannot be decided is marked unassessable and does not count as passed.

concepts.04-paired.description.text: Both versions run the same cases, and each case shows which one got better or worse; improvements and regressions both stay in the report.

section-1.title.text: One successful run does not make it usable

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: Only a fixed case set plus a holdout set can tell which of two versions is better. In {{lesson:task-contract}}, one task card and one run were enough for the acceptance checker to say whether that run passed. But after you change one sentence of the prompt, is the new version better or worse? One run cannot answer that: it may have gone well by luck and fail on another question, or the change may fix addition while breaking how division by zero is handled.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: Here is a made-up example. You add the rule "always call a tool for calculations", try "19 plus 23", get the right answer and decide the change works. The same rule may also make the assistant call add_numbers for nothing on a question whose answer is already given, such as "I ran 12 km this week and will run the same next week; how far is that?", or make it answer NONE whenever data is missing. Only when such situations are written down as a suite in advance, and the whole suite reruns after every change, do you see everything the change did.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: That is evaluation: measuring an agent with a fixed case set, criteria written in advance and an independent validator, and keeping every failure record. This lesson's suite is in cases.py. Each case states its category, how it should call tools and what the right answer is; the suite has a version, SUITE_VERSION, and each case a revision, rev. The cases come in two parts: the 6 you rerun while improving form the development set, and the other 4 form the holdout set, which nobody looks at or runs before a version is chosen. At the start of a run, lesson.task_card states which part runs and the suite's fingerprint.

section-1.paragraphs.3.text: Why set any cases aside? Tuning the prompt on the development set is like studying from the exam paper: getting everything right may only mean the prompt fits these 6 cases. The holdout set took no part in the changes, so its results come closer to "what happens on cases we have not seen". The price is that you may use it only sparingly: every time you look at its results and go back to change things, it becomes a second development set. A suite can be wrong too, and the public benchmarks in the references fixed many problems after release, so every change to the cases bumps the version, and scores from different versions are not compared directly.

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: Whatever a program can decide is decided by a program first, and the rules are written in a scoring sheet. An agent easily says "the task is done", but that sentence is not evidence. The acceptance checker of {{lesson:task-contract}} looked only at the task card and the tool results; this lesson scales the same idea up to a whole suite. verify in verifier.py takes exactly two things: the case spec, and the trace recorded in this run. It never calls a model and never reads the agent's opinion of itself.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: The scoring sheet is the spec of each case. In cases.py, add-basic says: call add_numbers once, with a as 19 and b as 23, and the answer is 42. clock-sum writes its arguments as references: the a of add_numbers must come from hour in the result of get_current_time, and b from minute. The right answer is also computed by the validator itself from the recorded hour and minute; it does not trust the value the agent's own addition returned. The final answer must end with a tag like `<answer>42</answer>`, or NONE when no number can be had, so that a program can read it.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: Rules written as a program have three advantages: the same trace gets the same verdict however often it is judged; judging a thousand cases costs no model call; and a wrong rule can be fixed like code and then regression-tested like code. Most public benchmarks in the references work this way: SWE-bench runs a test suite, GAIA uses exact string matching. Where a program cannot judge, this lesson does not force a verdict: for the open-ended self-introduction case greeting, the validator only checks that no tool was called for nothing, and the answer-correct check is marked unassessable.

section-2.paragraphs.3.text: Unassessable is not passed, and it must not quietly disappear either. The report counts it separately and keeps the case in the table, a reminder that this case needs a human or a calibrated judge model. Conversely, a wrong validator makes every score wrong, so this lesson's test_lesson.py first tests the validator against hand-written traces, one by one: correct traces must pass, while traces that guess arguments, invent numbers or report an answer without calling a tool must be stopped.

deep-dive-verifiers.title.text: How public benchmarks write their validators

deep-dive-verifiers.summary.text: Deterministic validators are cheap and reproducible, but they only say right or wrong, not at which step it went wrong.

deep-dive-verifiers.paragraphs.0.text: SWE-bench Verified splits "fixed" into two independent claims. One group of tests fails before the fix and passes after it, proving the problem is solved; another group passes both before and after, proving nothing else broke. Check only the first group and an agent can pass by deleting the assertions in its way; check only the second and you have checked nothing. This lesson follows the same idea: answer correct and no process violation are two checks, and one passing cannot vouch for the other.

deep-dive-verifiers.paragraphs.1.text: OSWorld's validators have full system access: for a database task they do not just check that a report file exists, they connect to the database and confirm the data was really written. GAIA makes answers impossible to look up directly online and then scores by exact match. τ²-bench states for every task the end-state assertions, the actions that must happen and the information the user must be told, and `reward_basis` decides which of them count. In one perfect-score trajectory the book analyzes, the agent broke the rule "call only one tool at a time", and the validator ignored it because that task was scored on the end state only.

deep-dive-verifiers.paragraphs.2.text: These validators share one cost: they give 0 or 1 but do not say where the failure began. That is why this lesson's report writes out the detail of every check besides the verdict, such as "Expected 1.5; answered 6" or "divide_numbers was sent before the result of get_current_time came back". In production, such failures are then attributed, the first step that went wrong is located, and the case becomes a new regression case.

deep-dive-verifiers.paragraphs.3.text: The book names three sources of cases. Public benchmarks screen models and lend design techniques, but their task distribution differs from your business, so two points gained there say little. A suite you build from your own tasks covers the real distribution and can back model choices and design decisions. Failures from production, found through user corrections, thumbs-down or checks after the fact, become regression cases after attribution; they cost the most and are the most accurate. The references describe the same loop: evaluate offline, deploy, collect new failures, add them to the offline suite, change, and repeat.

misconception-ended.claim.text: The run ended and the agent said it was done, so the case passed.

misconception-ended.correction.text: A run that ended only means the model gave a final answer. Each version's report in this lesson counts "runs ended" and "accepted" separately; answer, evidence and process are judged by the validator one by one. In the offline test mode script, version A ends all 6 development cases yet passes only 2; for real runs, your own report has the numbers.

predict-cases.prompt.text: Before you run "Development set: version A vs version B", guess: how many lesson.case_result events will this run produce?

mq-own-arithmetic.own-arithmetic.prompt.text: Why does the validator compute the right answer of clock-sum itself, adding hour and minute, instead of using the value the agent's add_numbers call returned?

mq-own-arithmetic.own-arithmetic.a.text.text: The agent's addition may have used guessed arguments, so its return value cannot be used to judge the agent

mq-own-arithmetic.own-arithmetic.a.feedb.text: Right. A number produced by the side being checked cannot be the standard it is checked against.

mq-own-arithmetic.own-arithmetic.b.text.text: The validator adds more accurately than the tool

mq-own-arithmetic.own-arithmetic.b.feedb.text: No. Both do the same addition; the difference is where the arguments come from.

mq-own-arithmetic.own-arithmetic.c.feedb.text: No. The addition tool does not fail in this case; the problem is that its arguments may be guesses.

mq-own-arithmetic.own-arithmetic.explana.text: The validator trusts only two things: the case spec and the clock result recorded in this run. It computes the answer from those itself.

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: Look beyond the final answer: check what was called and what the answer rests on. Looking only at the answer misses two kinds of error. One is the lucky guess: asked 19 plus 23, the agent calls no tool and writes 42 straight away. The answer is right but has no evidence at all, and next time, with larger numbers, it will do the arithmetic in its head again and may get it wrong. The other is doing it right but saying it wrong: the tool returned the right value, yet the final answer states a different number.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: So verify reports five checks for every case: run ended, call comparison, answer correct, evidence sufficient, and no process violation. check_evidence decides whether the evidence is sufficient: every number in the answer must appear in the question or in a successful tool result of this run. unknown-balance asks "What is my bank card balance plus 100 yuan?", and no tool can read a balance. If the answer is 1100, that number appears neither in the question nor in any tool result, and the evidence check fails. The rule borrows from the code accompanying the reference book: a number with no source cannot have come from evidence.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: find_violations decides whether there is a process violation, checking rules that hold whatever the answer is. The typical one is guessing arguments: clock-sum must read the time first and then add hour and minute. If add_numbers is sent in the same step as get_current_time, the addition's arguments can only be guesses. Every call in the trace records which step of the case it belongs to, step, so the validator can tell by comparing the two. Even a lucky guess does not make the case pass.

section-3.paragraphs.3.text: The checks cannot stand in for each other. divide-zero asks for 100 divided by 0. If the answer is 0 after the tool error, the evidence check lets it through, because 0 is written in the question; the violation check catches it, because after a tool error no number should be given. Conversely, sufficient evidence does not mean a right answer: the 42 computed from guessed arguments really is what add_numbers returned, so the evidence check passes while the answer is wrong. The evidence check shows that a number has a source, not that the source is the right one.

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: Before scoring with a judge model, check its agreement with human annotations. For an open-ended case like greeting, where a program cannot judge quality, the natural move is the judge model from {{lesson:prompt-experiments}}: write a rubric and let another model judge item by item. But the judge model makes mistakes too; before you take its verdicts at face value, compare them with a set of samples a human has already judged.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: This lesson's exercise "Judge model vs human annotation" does that with 6 fixed answers. The author wrote the answers and labeled each one pass or fail in advance; they are in JUDGE_SAMPLES in cases.py. The rubric has three items: name at least one real ability; claim no ability the assistant lacks; use one sentence. The runner sends each answer with the rubric to the model, reads back the verdict and compares it with the human label one by one. A reply in the wrong format counts as invalid, which is a disagreement.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: Agreement rate is not the only thing compared. The report splits disagreements into two kinds: a false pass, where the human said fail and the judge said pass, and a false fail, the other way round. The first is more dangerous because it counts bad answers into the pass rate. Sample j6 was written for exactly this: a long self-introduction whose first half is all correct, followed by "and I can also search the web for you". The reference book notes that judge models have a length bias and tend to score longer, more detailed answers higher; this sample is there to test it.

section-4.paragraphs.3.text: Six samples can only reveal obvious biases; they cannot prove the judge model reliable. Agreement rate can also be misled by class proportions: if 5 of the 6 samples pass, a judge that passes everything still agrees 83% of the time. That is why the report also gives `Cohen's kappa`, which removes the agreement expected by chance. Even a calibrated judge model is used only where a program cannot judge; checks that can be written as rules stay with the validator.

deep-dive-kappa.title.text: Computing agreement and kappa by hand

deep-dive-kappa.summary.text: Kappa answers one question: once chance agreement is removed, how much real skill does the judge model have left?

deep-dive-kappa.paragraphs.0.text: Suppose the judge model gets only j6 wrong among the 6 samples, passing it. The agreement rate is 5/6, about 0.83, which looks good. But first ask: how many would random guessing get right? The human annotations have 3 passes and 3 fails; the judge model gave 4 passes and 2 fails.

deep-dive-kappa.paragraphs.1.text: If the two sides were unrelated and each handed out verdicts at random in its own proportions, the chance of both saying pass would be `3/6 × 4/6 ≈ 0.33`, and of both saying fail `3/6 × 2/6 ≈ 0.17`, so chance agreement is about 0.5. Kappa is actual agreement minus chance agreement, divided by 1 minus chance agreement: `(0.83 − 0.5) ÷ 0.5 ≈ 0.67`. The kappa function computes exactly this formula.

deep-dive-kappa.paragraphs.2.text: 0.67 is usually read as "substantial agreement", but there are only 6 samples: one more wrongly judged passing sample and kappa drops to about 0.33. To be confident you need many more samples, covering every trap in the rubric. The reference book mentions two more practices: have several models from different families judge separately and see whether they agree; and when a judge model compares two candidates, judge twice with the order swapped, to cancel its tendency to favor one position.

mq-agreement.agreement.prompt.text: The judge model agrees with the human annotations on 5 of 6; the only disagreement is a long answer labeled fail that it passed. What is the safest course?

mq-agreement.agreement.a.text.text: Agreement is above 80%, so use it on every open-ended case

mq-agreement.agreement.a.feedback.text: No. There are too few samples, and it erred in the most dangerous direction.

mq-agreement.agreement.b.text.text: Read that misjudged answer first, find which kind of bias it shows, then add samples and calibrate again

mq-agreement.agreement.b.feedback.text: Right. A false pass inflates the pass rate; first find out why it happened.

mq-agreement.agreement.c.text.text: Change that sample's human label to pass

mq-agreement.agreement.c.feedback.text: No. Changing labels to raise agreement lets the judge model set the standard.

mq-agreement.agreement.explanation.text: Calibration is about finding where the judge model goes wrong, not about producing a good-looking agreement rate.

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: Parse the tool name and arguments before comparing, and sort calls into four kinds: simple, multiple, parallel and no call expected. The laziest approach compares the model's argument string with the expected string, but `{"a": 19, "b": 23}`, `{"b":23,"a":19}` and `{"a": 19.0, "b": 23}` are the same call with different strings. So same_call first parses the arguments into an object and then compares them one by one as numbers.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: By the shape of the calls, there are four common kinds. Simple: exactly one call, as in add-basic. Multiple: more than one candidate tool, and the right one must be picked; every case in this lesson offers all three tools, so picking the right tool runs through every case, and the dependent cases also require two different tools in order. Parallel: several independent calls in any order, as in two-sums, which needs two additions. No call expected: as in greeting and given-distance, where the right move is to call no tool at all.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: cases.py uses mode to pick the comparison rule: sequence requires the calls to match one to one and in the same order; unordered only requires every expected call to match a different actual call; none requires no call. Before comparing you must also decide which differences are not errors: swapping the two arguments of add_numbers does not change the result, so it is registered in COMMUTATIVE and both sides are sorted before comparing; 19 and 19.0 are equal as numbers. These decisions live in code, and every case and every version uses the same set.

section-5.paragraphs.3.text: Structured comparison only covers whether the calls were right, not whether their results were used right; that belongs to the answer-correct and evidence checks. It also accepts only the one approach the spec prescribes: if the agent first computes 19 ÷ 1 with divide_numbers and then adds, the result is right, yet the comparison still fails. The stricter the spec, the more likely a reasonable approach is judged wrong. The cases in this lesson are tiny and have only one reasonable approach; real tasks often write the acceptable calls as a set and list forbidden calls as well.

section-6.paragraphs.0.text: Run the same version several times to see its variance, and make a new version pass the old failure cases. Model output is random and the suite is small, so the gap between two versions may well be luck. A made-up example: on the 6 development cases, version A passes 2 and version B passes 5, which looks like a big jump; but every case ran only once, and one more run might change the verdicts.

section-6.paragraphs.1.text: First see how stable one version is on its own. The exercise "Same version, two runs" runs version B over the whole development set twice. The report lists each case's two verdicts, the number of cases passed both times (`Pass^2`) and the number passed at least once (`Pass@2`). The first is close to the reliability a business needs; the second only shows that it can be done. A case whose verdict differs between the two runs is varying on its own, so any difference between versions on that case should be discounted.

section-6.paragraphs.2.text: To compare two versions, use paired analysis: the same case, the same number of runs, only the version differs. paired compares the two versions' pass counts case by case and marks each as improved, regressed or unchanged; unchanged cases carry no information about the direction, so only the cases whose verdicts differ count. sign_test runs an exact sign test on those: if the two versions were equally good, the direction each differing case moves would be a coin flip. With fewer than 6 differing cases, even if all move the same way, the two-sided p-value cannot fall below 0.05, and the report says plainly that the difference is only a hint about direction.

section-6.paragraphs.3.text: Read every regression one by one. Suppose version B's "always call a tool for calculations" brings only improvements on the development set; the holdout set may still turn up a case like given-distance: the question already gives 12 km, yet the new rule makes the agent call a tool, and a case that used to pass no longer does. To call it a regression, check that version A passed the same case: if A also called the tool, the new rule did not cause it. Keep every regressed case and add it to the next version's regression check. When the report's check "Version B has no regression" fails, a higher total pass rate is no reason to ship. With several runs, paired still pairs by case and folds a case's runs into one verdict, instead of treating two runs of one case as two cases.

deep-dive-uncertainty.title.text: How uncertain a small sample really is

deep-dive-uncertainty.summary.text: A pass rate measured on 6 cases can be off by tens of percentage points either way.

deep-dive-uncertainty.paragraphs.0.text: The reference book gives a rough estimate: with pass rate `p` on `n` cases, the standard error is about `sqrt(p(1-p)/n)`. With 100 cases and a 70% pass rate, the 95% interval is about plus or minus 9 percentage points, so "73% for the new version against 70% for the old" is not enough to switch. With this lesson's 6 cases and a 50% pass rate, the standard error is about 0.2, and two standard errors either way is plus or minus 40 percentage points.

deep-dive-uncertainty.paragraphs.1.text: The formula breaks down for small samples and pass rates near 0 or 1: with all 6 passed, its interval has width 0, as if there were no doubt at all. That is why the report uses the Wilson interval, which the wilson function computes by its formula: 5 passes out of 6 give about 44% to 97%; 2 out of 6 give about 10% to 70%. The two intervals overlap widely, which already shows the versions cannot be told apart yet.

deep-dive-uncertainty.paragraphs.2.text: With several runs, also say which measure you mean. Suppose the runs are independent and a single run passes with probability 0.6. Over 5 runs, the chance of passing at least once is `1 − 0.4⁵ ≈ 99%`, while the chance of passing all 5 is only `0.6⁵ ≈ 7.8%`. The first number shows the upper limit of ability; only the second is close to the reliability that refunds or payments need. The repeat exercise in this lesson puts both numbers in the report so the flattering one cannot stand in for the unflattering one.

deep-dive-uncertainty.paragraphs.3.text: Both versions run the same cases, and a paired method is more sensitive than comparing two pass rates on their own. The reference book recommends McNemar's test or a paired bootstrap; the sign test in this lesson is the simplest method of that family: count only the cases whose verdicts differ and see whether improvements and regressions lean clearly to one side. With 3 cases all improved, the two-sided p-value is `2 × 0.5³ = 0.25`; only with 6 all improved does it drop to about 0.03. When several versions are compared at once, the chance of one good result appearing by luck also grows, so tighten the threshold or rerun the good result independently.

misconception-rate.claim.text: The pass rate went from 2/6 to 5/6, so the new version is better.

misconception-rate.correction.text: A pass rate over 6 cases has a large error, and the difference between two runs may be pure variance. Look at the paired verdicts: which cases improved, which regressed, and whether enough cases differ; then confirm on the holdout set and read every regressed case.

mq-sign-test.sign-test.prompt.text: In a paired analysis only 3 cases have different verdicts, all of them improvements, and the p-value is 0.25. What should the report say?

mq-sign-test.sign-test.a.text.text: Version B is significantly better and can ship

mq-sign-test.sign-test.a.feedback.text: No. All 3 cases going one way happens by coin flip a quarter of the time.

mq-sign-test.sign-test.b.text.text: The direction is consistent, but too few cases differ, so it is only a hint; confirm on the holdout set and enlarge the suite before concluding

mq-sign-test.sign-test.b.feedback.text: Right. That is exactly how this lesson's report reads when fewer than 6 cases differ.

mq-sign-test.sign-test.c.text.text: The two versions are equally good, so drop version B

mq-sign-test.sign-test.c.feedback.text: No. The evidence shows neither that B is better nor that the two are equal.

mq-sign-test.sign-test.explanation.text: With a small sample you can announce neither a significant difference nor no difference; what you can do is state the direction and the uncertainty honestly, then gather more evidence.

code-verify.n171.text.text: Process rules are independent of whether the answer is right: a lucky right answer still gets its violation recorded.

code-verify.n174.text.text: A tool name outside the allowlist is one violation of its own; the platform also refuses to run it.

code-verify.n178.text.text: Only expected calls with reference arguments have a source, such as the addition in clock-sum, which depends on the clock.

code-verify.n181.text.text: The step at which the source tool first returned successfully.

code-verify.n182.text.text: A dependent call sent in the same step as its source, or with no source result at all, can only have guessed arguments.

code-verify.n185.text.text: For a case that must answer NONE, giving a number after a tool error is inventing it.

code-verify.n190.text.text: The validator receives only the case spec and this run's trace, never the agent's self-assessment.

code-verify.n194.text.text: Run ended is a check of its own: the model gave a final answer, which does not mean it is right.

code-verify.n198.text.text: Without a final answer there is nothing to judge: answer correct fails outright and evidence does not apply.

code-verify.n201.text.text: Violations are the fifth check; the description of each one goes into detail.

code-compare-calls.n68.text.text: Compare one call: parse the arguments first, then compare the name and each argument as a number, never as a string.

code-compare-calls.n72.text.text: A different name, arguments that are not an object, a missing source or different argument names: the calls differ.

code-compare-calls.n74.text.text: For a commutative tool both sides are sorted before comparing, so swapping a and b is not an error.

code-compare-calls.n79.text.text: Other tools are compared argument by argument; 19 and 19.0 count as equal.

code-compare-calls.n82.text.text: Pick the comparison rule by the case's mode; return a status and the detail written into the report.

code-compare-calls.n85.text.text: A case with no call expected passes only with no call at all.

code-compare-calls.n87.text.text: Replace the case's references with values recorded in this run, for example hour with the 9 the clock returned.

code-compare-calls.n88.text.text: Without the source result the expected arguments cannot be determined, so the comparison fails.

code-compare-calls.n92.text.text: Simple and dependent cases: calls match one to one, in the same order.

code-compare-calls.n95.text.text: Parallel cases allow any order, but each actual call can match only one expected call, so repeating one call cannot fill two slots.

code-compare-calls.n104.text.text: On failure, the spec and the actual calls are written side by side, so the report shows at a glance what differs.

code-paired.n108r.text.text: Pair by case: same case, same number of runs, only the version differs.

code-paired.n113r.text.text: More passes is improved, fewer is regressed, the same is unchanged.

code-paired.n118r.text.text: Uses only the cases whose verdicts differ; unchanged cases say nothing about which version is better.

code-paired.n123r.text.text: The probability of a result at least this lopsided if both versions were equally good; times 2 gives the two-sided p-value.

code-decision.title.text: Program checks first, every failure kept, differences stated honestly

code-decision.chosen.text: Case specs live in cases.py, and the suite carries a version and a fingerprint; the validator reads only the spec and the trace, records five checks separately and marks what it cannot decide as unassessable; the two versions differ only in one paragraph of the prompt, are paired case by case, and a sign test states the uncertainty; open-ended cases calibrate the judge model first.

code-decision.self-report.title.text: Let the agent report in its answer whether it is done

code-decision.self-report.why_not.text: The side being checked grades itself, so lucky guesses and invented numbers both count as passed.

code-decision.judge-everything.title.text: Have the judge model score every case

code-decision.judge-everything.why_not.text: Costly, variable and biased; checks that can be written as rules are cheaper and more stable in a program.

code-decision.drop-unassessable.title.text: Drop the undecidable cases from the denominator

code-decision.drop-unassessable.why_not.text: The pass rate looks better, but the undecidable cases are exactly the ones that need a human.

code-decision.subtract-rates.title.text: Subtract the two pass rates and conclude

code-decision.subtract-rates.why_not.text: It hides which cases regressed and cannot say whether the difference is just variance.

version-compare.title.text: Version comparison: development and holdout sets

version-compare.hypothesis.text: The two versions differ only in one rule of the system prompt. On the development set, version B with the rule may improve on the tool-failure cases (version A may answer NONE without calling a tool); version A may already pass the dependent and missing-evidence cases. The holdout set checks whether the improvement is still there and whether a new regression appeared. Whatever the result, the five checks and the verdict of every case stay in the report.

version-compare.dev.label.text: Development set: version A vs version B

version-compare.holdout.label.text: Holdout set: one run once the version is chosen

version-compare.task-card.text.text: The task card: which cases run, the suite version and its fingerprint.

version-compare.violation.text.text: The first case with a violation, and what the violation was.

version-compare.ended.text.text: Runs ended, in a version's report.

version-compare.passed.text.text: Accepted cases, in the same report.

version-compare.regressed.text.text: The number of regressions in the paired analysis.

version-compare.guide.0.text.text: Both arms use the same validator: compare the two versions on the development set first, then run the holdout set once the version is chosen.

version-compare.guide.1.text.text: The task card states the suite version and fingerprint; change a case and the fingerprint changes.

version-compare.guide.2.text.text: Which process rule this case broke; even when the answer happens to be right, a violation means it did not pass.

version-compare.guide.3.text.text: An open-ended answer cannot be judged right or wrong, so it is unassessable: not passed, and not deleted either.

version-compare.guide.4.text.text: First see how many runs ended.

version-compare.guide.5.text.text: Then see how many were accepted: ending is not passing.

version-compare.guide.6.text.text: Regressions are cases version A passed and version B did not; if the number is not 0, read them one by one.

version-compare.guide.7.text.text: The p-value is for reference only; when too few cases differ, the report says it is only a hint about direction.

version-compare.conclusion.proves.0.text: Each case's five checks with their verdicts and reasons in this run, how the two versions changed case by case, and the sign test p-value computed from the record.

version-compare.conclusion.does_not_prov.text: Results on 6 or 4 cases do not show that version B is better on other tasks; the sample is too small and the p-value is for reference only.
The validator judges only by the case spec; if the spec itself is wrong, the verdicts are wrong too.
In offline test mode a fixed script plays both versions, and its improvements and regression are arranged by the script.

repeat-stability.hypothesis.text: With the same version and the same cases, and a request that asks for temperature 0 (omitted when the model does not support it; see omitted_params), two runs may still not give exactly the same verdicts; a case whose verdict flips shows that differences on that case are within variance.

repeat-stability.second-run.text.text: The first case of the second pass.

repeat-stability.unstable.text.text: Cases whose verdict changed between runs.

repeat-stability.guide.0.text.text: Version B runs the whole development set twice, so every case gets two verdicts.

repeat-stability.guide.1.text.text: The second pass starts again from the first case, sending the same requests as the first.

repeat-stability.guide.2.text.text: Only passing both times counts as a stable pass.

repeat-stability.guide.3.text.text: Passing at least once shows it can be done, not that it can be relied on.

repeat-stability.guide.4.text.text: When some verdicts flip, differences between versions on those cases should be discounted.

repeat-stability.conclusion.proves.0.text: Whether each case got the same verdict in these two runs, and how many cases passed both times and at least once.

repeat-stability.conclusion.does_not_pro.text: Two identical runs do not mean every run is identical; two runs only catch obvious variance.
The offline test mode script is deterministic, so its two passes always agree; real variance needs a real run.

judge-calibration.hypothesis.text: With a specific rubric, most of the judge model's verdicts agree with the human annotations; when a long answer hides a false claim, it may pass it.

judge-calibration.judge-request.text.text: The rubric sent to the judge model.

judge-calibration.judgement.text.text: One judgement: the sample, the human label, the judge's verdict and whether they agree.

judge-calibration.guide.0.text.text: Six fixed answers go to the judge model one at a time, each with a human annotation the author wrote in advance.

judge-calibration.guide.1.text.text: The system prompt holds the rubric; the judge model outputs only a verdict and a one-sentence reason.

judge-calibration.guide.2.text.text: Each judgement is compared with the human label, and agree records whether they match.

judge-calibration.guide.3.text.text: The agreement rate is the most direct number.

judge-calibration.guide.4.text.text: False passes are the most dangerous: bad answers get counted into the pass rate.

judge-calibration.guide.5.text.text: Kappa removes chance agreement, and with few samples it swings widely.

judge-calibration.conclusion.proves.0.text: This run's judge model verdict on each answer, plus its agreement with the human annotations, the number of false passes and kappa.

judge-calibration.conclusion.does_not_pr.text: Six samples cannot prove the judge model reliable, nor carry over to other rubrics or cases.
The human annotations were written by the author and may themselves be disputed.
In offline test mode a script gives the verdicts, and the misjudgment of j6 is arranged by the script.

inputs.task.options.compare.label.text: Run the suite and compare versions

inputs.split.help.text: 6 development cases, 4 holdout cases; used only when comparing versions.

inputs.versions.help.text: The two versions differ only in one paragraph of rules in the system prompt.

inputs.versions.options.both.label.text: Both versions, with a paired analysis

inputs.repeats.help.text: Run the whole suite 1 or 2 times; each case uses at most 3 model calls, and the run checks up front that it stays within this lesson's call limit.

quiz.q1.prompt.text: Why does the holdout set run only once, after the version is chosen?

quiz.q1.a.text.text: Every time you look at its results and go back to change things, it becomes a second development set

quiz.q1.a.feedback.text: Right. A holdout set is worth something because it was never used to adjust the version.

quiz.q1.b.text.text: Holdout cases are harder than development cases

quiz.q1.b.feedback.text: No. Nothing says which part is harder; the difference is how they are used.

quiz.q1.c.text.text: The holdout set needs no validator

quiz.q1.c.feedback.text: No. Both parts use the same validator.

quiz.q1.explanation.text: Scores on the development set grow more optimistic with every change; the holdout set is there to correct that optimism.

quiz.q2.prompt.text: In clock-sum, the agent sends get_current_time and add_numbers in the same step and happens to get the answer right. How does the validator judge it?

quiz.q2.a.feedback.text: No. A right answer does not mean a right process.

quiz.q2.b.text.text: Failed: the addition was sent before the clock result came back, so its arguments could only be guesses

quiz.q2.b.feedback.text: Right. find_violations compares the step of the two calls.

quiz.q2.c.feedback.text: No. The clock result exists, so the right answer can be computed and the violation can be judged.

quiz.q2.explanation.text: No process violation is a check of its own, and a lucky right answer cannot save it.

quiz.q3.prompt.text: The answer to unknown-balance is 1100. Besides answer correct, which check fails?

quiz.q3.a.text.text: Evidence sufficient: 1100 appears neither in the question nor in any tool result

quiz.q3.a.feedback.text: Right. The number has no source at all.

quiz.q3.b.feedback.text: No. The model gave a final answer, so the run did end.

quiz.q3.c.feedback.text: No. The case expects no tool call, and none was made.

quiz.q3.explanation.text: An invented number cannot pass the evidence check; this is exactly what check_evidence is there to stop.

quiz.q4.prompt.text: greeting is marked unassessable. Which handling is right?

quiz.q4.a.text.text: Remove it from the suite so it does not drag the pass rate down

quiz.q4.a.feedback.text: No. Removing undecidable cases turns the pass rate into a hand-picked number.

quiz.q4.b.text.text: Count it separately, keep it in the report, and leave it to a human or a calibrated judge model

quiz.q4.b.feedback.text: Right. Unassessable has to be reported as it is.

quiz.q4.c.text.text: Nothing is wrong with it, so count it as passed

quiz.q4.c.feedback.text: No. Finding no error is not the same as having checked.

quiz.q4.explanation.text: Unassessable means the validator lacks information; the way to supply it is a human or a judge model, not a different way of counting.

quiz.q5.prompt.text: Of 6 samples, the human annotations pass 5 and fail 1; the judge model passes all of them, for 83% agreement. Why look at kappa as well?

quiz.q5.a.text.text: Passing everything already reaches 83%; kappa removes the agreement expected by chance

quiz.q5.a.feedback.text: Right. Here kappa is 0: the judge model added no information.

quiz.q5.b.text.text: Kappa is always higher than the agreement rate

quiz.q5.b.feedback.text: No. Kappa is usually lower than the agreement rate.

quiz.q5.c.feedback.text: No. Kappa itself is computed from human annotations.

quiz.q5.explanation.text: When classes are lopsided, the agreement rate overrates the judge model; kappa removes that part.

quiz.q6.prompt.text: add_numbers is registered in COMMUTATIVE. What does that mean?

quiz.q6.a.text.text: Swapping a and b is not an error in the comparison

quiz.q6.a.feedback.text: Right. Swapping the arguments of an addition does not change the result.

quiz.q6.b.text.text: It may be called in parallel with other tools

quiz.q6.b.feedback.text: No. Whether calls may run in parallel depends on the case's mode and its dependencies.

quiz.q6.c.feedback.text: No. The answer and the evidence are checked as usual.

quiz.q6.explanation.text: Before a structured comparison, write down which differences are not errors, and compare every case by the same rules.

quiz.q7.prompt.text: In a paired analysis, version B improves 2 cases and regresses 1, and its total pass rate is higher than version A's. What is the best next step?

quiz.q7.a.text.text: The total pass rate went up, so ship it

quiz.q7.a.feedback.text: No. The regressed case shows the new rule has a side effect on some kind of case.

quiz.q7.b.text.text: Read the regressed case, find the cause, and add it to the next version's regression check

quiz.q7.b.feedback.text: Right. Regressed cases are the most direct lead for the next round of changes.

quiz.q7.c.text.text: Remove the regressed case from the suite

quiz.q7.c.feedback.text: No. Removing failed cases hides the problem.

quiz.q7.explanation.text: Improvements and regressions both stay in the report; regressed cases especially are kept to check later versions.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Run "Development set: version A vs version B" and find the first case with a process violation.

check-hunt.explanation.text: The violations of lesson.case_result list the process rules this case broke, each with an id and a description; guessed_dependency, for example, means a dependent call was sent before its source result came back. In the same event's checks, no process violation is failed and so is the case verdict, even if answer correct passed. If this run had no violation at all, the page tells you the evidence is missing.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare with your own run and this lesson's source, and tick only what you have done.

check-points.item-1.text.text: I compared runs ended with accepted in a version's report and can say why they differ.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I found a failed case, read the detail of each of its checks, and can say at which step it went wrong.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I looked at the improvements, regressions and p-value of the paired analysis and can write a one-sentence conclusion that does not overstate.

check-points.item-4.text.text: I read every judge verdict and its reason; where they disagreed I judged which way it leaned, and where they did not I can say what 6 agreeing samples do not prove.

code_notes.verify.note.text: The validator's entry point: reads only the case spec and this run's trace, and gives five checks and a case verdict.

code_notes.check_evidence.note.text: Evidence check: every number in the answer must appear in the question or a successful tool result of this run.

code_notes.find_violations.note.text: Process rules: unregistered tools, dependent calls sent before their source result, numbers given after a tool error.

code_notes.same_call.note.text: Compares one call after parsing its arguments as numbers; commutative tools ignore argument order.

code_notes.COMMUTATIVE.note.text: Tools whose arguments may be swapped; in this lesson only add_numbers.

code_notes.mode.note.text: Call comparison rule: sequence matches one to one in order, unordered in any order, none expects no call.

code_notes.step.note.text: Which model call of the case a call belongs to; calls sent in the same step cannot see each other's results.

code_notes.rev.note.text: A case's revision; bump it whenever that case's spec changes.

code_notes.SUITE_VERSION.note.text: The suite version; adding or removing cases or changing a spec bumps it, and scores of different versions are not compared directly.

code_notes.paired.note.text: Compares the two versions' pass counts case by case, marking improved, regressed and unchanged.

code_notes.sign_test.note.text: An exact sign test over only the cases whose verdicts differ, giving a two-sided p-value.

code_notes.wilson.note.text: Wilson interval: a pass-rate interval that stays between 0 and 1 even for tiny samples.

code_notes.JUDGE_SAMPLES.note.text: Calibration samples: 6 answers written by the author with their human annotations; not run records.

code_notes.lesson.case_result.note.text: One run of one case: five checks, violations, failed checks and unassessable checks.

code_notes.verdict.note.text: The judge model's verdict; only pass or fail counts, anything else is invalid.
